items.title: optimized-svm
items.text:
Project website

Interactive explainers, benchmarks and a summary of the thesis: wotzlaff.github.io/svm-site — Explore · Benchmarks

Support vector machines whose hyperparameters are tuned by exact gradients instead of grid search.

optimized-svm treats hyperparameter selection as a bilevel optimization problem: the upper level minimizes a (smoothed) cross-validation error, the lower level is the SVM training problem. Smoothing the loss makes the training solution differentiable in the hyperparameters, so the gradient of the CV error follows from the implicit function theorem and a quasi-Newton method (L-BFGS-B) can be used. This works for the regularization parameter and for per-feature kernel scalings (automatic relevance determination), where grid search is hopeless.

The methods are developed in

N. Strasdat, Duality, Derivative-Based Training Methods and Hyperparameter Optimization for Support Vector Machines, Dissertation, Technische Universität Dresden, 2023. urn:nbn:de:bsz:14-qucosa2-874731

Training uses the Rust SMO solver smo-solver as a warm start followed by a semismooth Newton method on the smoothed primal problem.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• scikit-learn estimators: OptimizedSVC, OptimizedSVR (tuned) and SmoothSVC, SmoothSVR (fixed hyperparameters); binary and one-vs-rest classification
  • losses: smoothed hinge, logistic (with predict_proba), smoothed ε-insensitive, squared (LS-SVM), Poisson; smoothing of degree 2, 3 or 6; sample/class weights; optional bound on Σ|α| (generalized ν-SVM)
  • exact hypergradients via one adjoint linear system per fold (verified against finite differences), also with respect to the loss parameters ε and δ (low-level API)
  • ARD kernels (blocks="features") with two-stage optimization, warm starts, time limits, full optimization history
  • decision_gradient() for local feature sensitivities

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pip install optimized-svm

For development (the solver smo-solver is installed from PyPI as a prebuilt wheel):

git clone https://github.com/wotzlaff/optimized-svm && cd optimized-svm
uv sync --group dev
uv run pytest

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVR

x, y = make_friedman1(600, noise=0.5, random_state=0)
model = OptimizedSVR(blocks="features").fit(x, y)   # one kernel scaling per feature

model.lam_            # optimized regularization parameter
model.scaling_opt_    # optimized scalings: features 5..9 (pure noise) are switched off
model.history_        # every evaluation of the CV error
model.predict(x[:5])

On a 1000-sample classification task (examples/quickstart.py) the optimizer needs 16 CV evaluations (≈1 s) versus 143 grid points (≈13 s) for GridSearchCV with sklearn.svm.SVC, with comparable test accuracy (0.844 vs. 0.856). More comparisons: Benchmarks.

items.text: step method thesis training, warm start SMO on the dual with quadratic smoothing (smo-solver) Ch. 7 training, refinement semismooth Newton on a + φ'(Ka/λ + b + sc) = 0 Ch. 8.4 CV error gradient implicit function theorem, adjoint system per fold Ch. 9.2 hyperparameter search L-BFGS-B over (log λ, log s₁, …, log s_K) Ch. 9.1, 10.4

items.title: optimized_svm.train(prob, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, alpha0=None)
items.text:
Two-step training: SMO warm start followed by Newton refinement.

For non-smooth losses (smoothing = 0) the SMO solution is already exact; for losses without SMO formulation (squared, logistic, Poisson) Newton starts at zero.

By default the SMO stage stops at the tolerance :data:ROUGH_SMO_TOL or after ROUGH_SMO_STEPS steps per loss term, whichever comes first. Passing tol or max_steps in smo_options replaces these defaults (no step budget then).

items.text:
Damped semismooth Newton method for the (smoothed) primal training problem.

Requires a loss with (piecewise) second derivative. The 1-norm constraint is treated as active iff c > 0 at the starting point.

items.title: optimized_svm.losses
items.text:
Loss functions of the training problem, expressed per loss term.

A training problem with n samples consists of m loss terms: one per sample, or two for the epsilon-insensitive loss (one for each side of the tube). Term l belongs to sample kernel_index[l], has weight w_l, label y_l and sign s_l (used by the optional 1-norm constraint, 0 if not applicable). The decision value of a term is f(x_l) + s_l c.

items.title: Terms dataclass
items.text: Term structure of a training problem.

items.title: Loss
items.text: Base class: per-term loss phi_l(t) and its derivatives.

items.title: param_ratio(name, t, terms)
items.text:
(d phi'_l / d p) / phi''_l at fixed t for the loss parameter p = name.

Only meaningful for terms with positive curvature; it is the sensitivity of the optimality condition a_l + phi'_l(t_l) = 0 w.r.t. p in units of t and is used by the hypergradient with respect to loss parameters.

items.title: HingeLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Smoothed hinge loss w * m_delta(shift - y t) for labels y in {-1, +1}.

items.title: LogisticLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Logistic loss w * log(1 + exp(-y t)) for y in {-1, +1} (Strasdat, Sec. 4.1.3).

Smooth without a smoothing parameter and strictly convex, but with positive curvature everywhere: the dual solution is dense and the dual is not a separable quadratic, so there is no SMO warm start and every Newton system has the full size n.

items.title: EpsilonInsensitiveLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Smoothed epsilon-insensitive loss w * (m(y - t - eps) + m(t - y - eps)).

Uses two terms per sample: sign +1 for m(y - t - eps) and -1 for the other side.

items.title: SquaredLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Least-squares loss w / 2 * (t - y)^2 (LS-SVM).

items.title: PoissonLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Poisson negative log-likelihood w * (exp(t) - y t + log(y!)) for counts y.

items.title: ApproxPoissonLoss dataclass
items.text:
Bases: Loss

Poisson-type loss with a linear left tail (from the original experiments):

w * (exp(t) - (y + 1) t - 1 + log(y!)) for t > 0 and w * (-y t + log(y!)) else.

It is convex and continuously differentiable; for t <= 0 its curvature vanishes.

items.title: optimized_svm.cv_error_and_gradient(theta, x, y, w, folds, loss, validation, blocks=None, max_asum=None, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, warm_start=None, loss_params=(), basis=None)
items.text:
Mean validation error over all folds and its gradient w.r.t. theta.

theta = (log lam, log s_1, ..., log s_K, log p_1, ...): regularization, kernel scalings and the values of the loss parameters named in loss_params (fields of loss such as "epsilon" or "smoothing"; they replace the values stored in loss).

warm_start is a list with one (possibly None) start vector per fold; it is updated in place with the new solutions.

With basis (one array of sample indices per fold, indices into x) every fold trains a Subspace SVM whose model is spanned by these basis points (:mod:optimized_svm.subspace); warm_start then holds expansion coefficients instead of dual variables. Loss parameters and the 1-norm constraint are not supported in that case.

items.title: optimized_svm.fold_error_and_gradient(x_train, y_train, w_train, x_val, y_val, loss, validation, lam, blocks, max_asum=None, smo_options=None, newton_options=None, alpha0=None, loss_params=())
items.text:
Validation error of one fold and its gradient w.r.t. (log lam, log s_k, log p_j).

p_j are the loss parameters named in loss_params (e.g. "epsilon", "smoothing"), taken from loss. x_train/x_val must already be scaled.

items.title: optimized_svm.subspace
items.text:
Subspace SVM: training and hypergradient in a low-dimensional subspace (Strasdat, Sec. 5.3).

The model is restricted to the subspace spanned by m basis points z_1, ..., z_m::

w = sum_j beta_j phi(z_j),    f(x) = sum_j beta_j k(x, z_j) + b.

By Corollary 5.9 the dual of this problem is the standard dual with the projected kernel K_s = K_XZ K_ZZ^{-1} K_ZX (a Nystroem approximation), so a Subspace SVM is an SVM with the explicit finite-dimensional feature map psi(x) = L^{-1} k_Z(x) where K_ZZ = L L^T. The primal problem has only m + 1 unknowns,

min_{u, b}  lam/2 |u|^2 + sum_l phi_l(psi_{k(l)}^T u + b),        beta = L^{-T} u,

and is solved by a damped Newton method with systems of size m + 1 instead of n: cost O(n m^2 + m^3) per step. Losses must have positive curvature somewhere (smoothed hinge or epsilon-insensitive loss with smoothing > 0, squared, logistic, Poisson); SMO is not used.

The hypergradient of the cross-validation error w.r.t. log lam and the log kernel scalings follows from the implicit function theorem for the stationarity conditions in (beta, b); one adjoint system of size m + 1 is solved per fold (derivation in docs/theory/subspace.md).

items.title: choose_basis(n, m, seed=0)
items.text: Random subset of m out of n sample indices (sorted).

items.title: select_basis(x, lam, tol=1.0, max_size=None)
items.text:
Greedy pivoted Cholesky of the RBF kernel on scaled features x.

Adds the sample with the largest remaining kernel variance until the absolute trace of the Nystroem residual tr(K - K_s) is at most tol * lam or max_size points are chosen (default max(10, n // 10)). Returns the sorted indices and the final tr(K - K_s) / lam; a value above tol means that the size limit was hit and the subspace model is not a close approximation (the study in benchmarks/subspace_params.py found a cross-validation error at most 1 % above the full model for tol = 1 and at most 14 % for tol = 10).

items.title: nystroem_residual(x, idx)
items.text: Trace of the Nystroem residual tr(K - K_s) of the RBF kernel on scaled features x for the basis x[idx], i.e. n - ||psi||_F^2 with psi = K_XZ L^-T and L the Cholesky factor of the jittered K_ZZ (as in :class:SubspaceProblem). Clipped at 0.

items.title: newton_subspace(prob, beta0=None, b0=0.0, **options)
items.text:
Damped Newton method for the subspace problem (m + 1 unknowns).

A warm start (beta0, b0) may lie in a region where the loss is linear in all samples (tiny lam gives huge coefficients), so the Hessian is just lam I and no step is accepted. The solve is then repeated from the cold start u = 0, b = 0, which is always well-posed; a :class:ConvergenceError of the cold start is raised.

items.title: optimized_svm.validation
items.text:
Validation error measures E(f) = sum_v L_v(f_v) for the upper level problem (Sec. 9.1.4).

All measures are differentiable so that the hyperparameter objective has a gradient.

items.title: ValidationLoss

sum_v w_v log(1 + exp(-y_v f_v)); balanced weights both classes equally.

Smoothed absolute error sum_v m_delta(f_v - y_v) + m_delta(y_v - f_v) (Huber-like).

1/2 sum_v (f_v - y_v)^2.

items.title: PoissonValidation dataclass

Poisson deviance-type loss sum_v exp(f_v) - y_v f_v + log(y_v!).

items.title: optimized_svm.kernels
items.text:
Gaussian kernel with feature scaling and its derivatives w.r.t. log-scalings.

The hyperparameters of the kernel are scalings s_k > 0 of feature blocks B_k: k(x, z) = exp(-sum_k s_k^2 |x_{B_k} - z_{B_k}|^2). With a single block this is the RBF kernel with gamma = s^2; with one block per feature it is an ARD kernel. The training code works on scaled features x_{B_k} * s_k and an RBF kernel with gamma = 1.

items.title: squared_distances(x, z)
items.text: Matrix of squared Euclidean distances |x_i - z_j|^2 (clipped at zero).

items.title: rbf(x, z)
items.text: exp(-|x - z|^2) for already scaled features.

items.title: rbf_with_gradient(x, z, blocks=None)
items.text:
Kernel matrix and its derivatives w.r.t. the log-scalings of all blocks.

Returns K of shape (n, m) and dK of shape (n, m, n_blocks) with dK[..., k] = d K / d log s_k = -2 K * |x_{B_k} - z_{B_k}|^2 (features already scaled).

items.title: contract_gradient(x, z, k, left, right, blocks=None)
items.text:
Bilinear forms left^T (dK / d log s_k) right with dK_k = -2 K * |x_Bk - z_Bk|^2.

k is the kernel matrix between the (already scaled) points x and z. Same as contracting the output of :func:rbf_with_gradient, but without forming the distance matrices of the blocks: with W = K * left right^T one has sum_ij W_ij |x_i - z_j|^2 = rowsum(W) . |x|^2 + colsum(W) . |z|^2 - 2 sum(x * (W z)) per feature, so a single matrix product serves all blocks.

items.title: scale_features(x, scaling, blocks=None)
items.text: Multiplies the features of each block by its scaling.

items.title: optimized_svm.smooth_max
items.text:
Smooth approximations of the maximum function max(0, t) (Strasdat, Sec. 4.4).

Each approximation m_delta coincides with max(0, t) for |t| >= delta and is a polynomial on (-delta, delta). The degree determines the smoothness:

  • "2": C^1, piecewise quadratic (its conjugate is quadratic, so SMO applies),
  • "3": C^2, piecewise cubic,
  • "6": C^2, a single sextic polynomial on (-delta, delta).

items.title: smooth_max(delta, degree='2')
items.text:
Returns (m, dm, ddm): the smoothed maximum and its first two derivatives.

delta = 0 yields the (non-smooth) maximum itself.

items.text: • Documentation built with Zensical instead of MkDocs Material (zensical.toml); the example scripts are executed by scripts/build_examples.py before the build (Zensical has no mkdocs-jupyter). API reference: new section for optimized_svm.subspace.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Subspace SVM (thesis Sec. 5.3), experimental: optimized_svm.subspace (Newton training in the span of \(m\) basis points, systems of size \(m+1\)) and the basis argument of cv_error_and_gradient with an exact hypergradient (checked against finite differences). select_basis chooses the basis points by pivoted Cholesky until the Nyström residual trace is at most tol * lam; nystroem_residual. The estimators take n_basis (int or "auto") and basis_tol; with "auto" the optimizers re-select the basis (up to 5 rounds per stage, basis_round in history_) when the residual exceeds basis_tol * lam at the result of L-BFGS-B. Studies: benchmarks/subspace_params.py, subspace_large.py, subspace_hpo.py. Pays off for fits with fixed hyperparameters at large \(n\); in the optimizers no gain without loss of accuracy so far; see theory/subspace.md.
  • Benchmark scripts benchmarks/hpo_vs_search.py (gradient method against grid, random and successive-halving search) and benchmarks/hpo_timing.py (wall-clock time of complete optimizations, for comparing releases). Results: https://wotzlaff.github.io/svm-site/benchmarks/
  • Hypergradient with respect to the loss parameters epsilon and smoothing: loss_params of cv_error_and_gradient/fold_error_and_gradient and Loss.param_ratio. Exact (checked against finite differences), but not used by the estimators: tuning these parameters rarely pays off (epsilon is not identifiable below the smoothing width, the CV error is multimodal in smoothing). Study: benchmarks/hpo_loss_params.py.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • cv_error_ of the optimizers is the cross-validation error at the returned hyperparameters (before: the minimum over history_; the same value except with re-selected subspace bases).

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • newton_subspace repeats the solve from a cold start when a warm start with huge coefficients (tiny lam) gives no descent step.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • Switch from SMO to Newton: the rough SMO stage now stops at tolerance 0.3 (was 0.1) or after five steps per loss term. Same results; ε-SVR hyperparameter optimization up to 2.5 times faster, and 1–2 orders of magnitude faster with an active 1-norm bound, where SMO converges very slowly. Explicit tol/max_steps in smo_options replace the defaults. Study: benchmarks/smo_newton_switch.py.

items.title: Added
items.text: • smo_options accepts the bound-aware stopping criterion of smo-solver (stopping="bound_aware", rho); requires smo-solver>=0.1.2.

items.title: Added
items.text: • Logistic loss (thesis Sec. 4.1.3): LogisticLoss, LogisticValidation and loss="logistic" for SmoothSVC/OptimizedSVC, including predict_proba (sigmoid of the decision values, normalised one-vs-rest probabilities for more than two classes). Trained by Newton's method only, the solution is dense; max_asum is not supported. Hypergradients are covered by the finite-difference tests.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Faster hypergradient: kernel matrices are handled per sample (ε-SVR uses n instead of 2n columns), the validation kernel columns are reused for the adjoint system, and the kernel derivatives are contracted per block with one matrix product instead of forming a distance matrix per block.
  • The Cholesky factor of the last Newton system is reused for the adjoint system when the curvature pattern is unchanged (always the case for smoothing of degree 2).
  • Linear systems of size up to 1000 are factorized with a single BLAS thread; multi-threaded LAPACK was several times slower for them, notably on shared machines. New dependency: threadpoolctl.
  • Typical effect (ε-SVR, n = 450, 5-fold, one BLAS thread): 3.2 s → 2.0 s; ARD 2.0 s → 0.9 s; classification (n = 600) 1.3 s → 0.7 s. Results are unchanged.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • Warm starts were counterproductive for classification: repairing the rounding error of sum(alpha) = 0 moved a third of the variables off their bounds and made SMO take about four times as many steps as a cold start. Now about four times fewer than a cold start.
Complete overhaul of the 2022 code (tag legacy-2022).

items.title: Classification
items.text:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVC

x, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
x = StandardScaler().fit_transform(x)
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, random_state=0)

clf = OptimizedSVC(cv=5, verbose=1).fit(x_train, y_train)
print(clf.lam_, clf.scaling_opt_, clf.score(x_test, y_test))

OptimizedSVC minimizes the 5-fold cross-validation error of a smoothed hinge loss over \(\log\lambda\) and the log kernel scaling \(\log s\) (the RBF parameter is \(\gamma = s^2\)). After the search the model is refitted on all data with the best parameters.

Feature scaling

The kernel acts on the raw features. Standardize them (e.g. with StandardScaler) or use blocks="features" so that every feature gets its own scaling.

items.title: Regression and feature relevance
items.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVR

x, y = make_friedman1(600, noise=0.5, random_state=0)
reg = OptimizedSVR(epsilon=0.1, blocks="features").fit(x, y)
print(reg.scaling_opt_.round(3))   # small values = irrelevant features

With blocks="features" the kernel is \(k(x, z) = \exp(-\sum_j s_j^2 (x_j - z_j)^2)\). With two_stage=True (default) a single common scaling is optimized first and used as starting point.

items.title: Choosing the model
items.text:
estimator loss parameters SmoothSVC / OptimizedSVC (loss="hinge") smoothed hinge \(w_i\, m_\delta(\text{shift} - y_i f(x_i))\) smoothing, degree, shift, class_weight, max_asum loss="logistic" \(w_i \log(1 + e^{-y_i f(x_i)})\), enables predict_proba class_weight SmoothSVR / OptimizedSVR (loss="epsilon_insensitive") \(w_i (m_\delta(f_i - y_i - \varepsilon) + m_\delta(y_i - f_i - \varepsilon))\) epsilon, smoothing, degree loss="squared" \(\tfrac{w_i}{2} (f_i - y_i)^2\) (LS-SVM) – loss="poisson" \(w_i (e^{f_i} - y_i f_i)\), prediction \(e^{f}\) –

The logistic loss needs no smoothing, but it yields a dense solution and is trained by Newton's method only, so every training step solves a system of size \(n\): prefer the hinge loss for large \(n\) unless you need probabilities. It does not support max_asum.

smoothing (\(\delta\)) controls how strongly the kinks of the loss are rounded; degree selects the smoothing polynomial ("2": \(C^1\), exactly solvable by SMO; "3" and "6": \(C^2\)).

items.title: Useful attributes
items.text:
• lam_, scaling_opt_: optimized hyperparameters
  • history_: list of all CV evaluations (lam, scaling, error, gradient_norm, time, …)
  • cv_error_, time_, n_iter_
  • support_, dual_coef_, intercept_, training_info_ of the final model
  • decision_gradient(X): derivative of the decision function w.r.t. the inputs

items.title: Lower-level building blocks
items.text:
from optimized_svm import EpsilonInsensitiveLoss, TrainingProblem, train

prob = TrainingProblem(x * 0.5, y, EpsilonInsensitiveLoss(0.1, 0.05, "3"), lam=1e-3)
sol = train(prob)          # SMO warm start + Newton refinement
sol.a, sol.b, sol.residual

See examples/ in the repository for complete scripts.

items.title: Reproducing the thesis
items.text:
benchmarks/thesis_regression.py follows the protocol of Sec. 10.4.2:

  • LIBSVM regression datasets (downloaded and cached on first use),
  • 30 random splits, 80 % for hyperparameter optimization and training, 20 % for testing,
  • features and targets standardized on the training part,
  • smoothed \(\varepsilon\)-SVR with cubic smoothing (\(\delta = \varepsilon/4\)) for \(\varepsilon \in \{0.1, 0.25, 0.5\}\) and the LS-SVM,
  • 5-fold CV with the smoothed absolute validation error (\(\delta = 0.1\)),
  • start \(\lambda = 10^{-2}\), \(\gamma = \log 2 / d\); bounds \(\lambda \in [10^{-6}, 1]\), \(\gamma \in [10^{-12}, 10^4]\); time limit 600 s,
  • datasets with more than 1000 samples are subsampled to 1000.
python benchmarks/thesis_regression.py --splits 30

items.title: Diagnosis of the mpg/housing deviation
items.text:
• Not the optimizer. A dense GridSearchCV over (C, γ) (SVR) or KernelRidge (LS-SVM) with the same standardization and CV reaches the same test error on the same 30 splits: mpg 7.84 ± 0.36 (SVR grid) and 7.51 (LS-SVM, identical to ours); housing 10.9 (LS-SVM grid, ours 10.85). The gradient method therefore does not get stuck in a poor local minimum, and for the LS-SVM the implementation agrees with an independent solver.
  • Split noise contributes but does not explain it alone. The per-split MSE of mpg has a standard deviation of about 2; the mean over 30 splits varies by roughly ±0.4. For mpg the thesis value lies about 2 standard errors below ours, but housing deviates in the same direction.
  • Binarising nominal features does not help. The OpenML versions of the data sets (autoMpg, id 196; boston, id 531) have nominal columns (mpg: cylinders, model, origin; housing: CHAS, RAD). One-hot encoding them (mpg: 7 → 25 columns, housing: 13 → 22) makes the results worse (mpg LS-SVM 7.96, housing LS-SVM 11.54).

  • Different protocols are not comparable. The 2018/19 runs of hpo4svm on OpenML use the 10-fold CV of the OpenML tasks (3/5/10 inner folds). A 10-fold CV of a KernelRidge grid on the LIBSVM data gives MAE 1.87 (mpg) and 2.09 (housing), close to our values.

  • The old code does not reproduce the splits. The 2018/19 prototype hpo4svm draws its splits with np.random.seed(42) and np.random.permutation; replaying that sequence on the LIBSVM files (datasets in the order pyrim, triazines, mpg, housing) does not reproduce Table 10.4.1 (pyrim LS-SVM MSE 0.0100 instead of 0.0060, mpg 8.37 instead of 6.63). That script is a later experiment (3-fold CV, different bounds); the script that produced the table and the input files (~/daten/regression/<name>/data.mat) are not available.

The cause of the deviation remains open. Remaining candidates are the exact data set versions and preprocessing used in the thesis (not documented there; the protocol is adopted from Fischer et al., Optim. Methods Softw. 30(6), 2015) and the specific random splits.

items.title: Class probabilities with the logistic loss
items.text:
loss="logistic" trains the SVM with the logistic loss of the thesis (Sec. 4.1.3) and enables predict_proba. We tune it with OptimizedSVC and compare it with the smoothed hinge loss, whose decision values we pass through a sigmoid for the comparison.

The logistic loss needs no SMO warm start and gives a dense solution, so every Newton system has the full size n: it is the slower of the two and meant for moderate n.

import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVC

x, y = make_classification(800, 8, n_informative=4, flip_y=0.1, random_state=0)
x = StandardScaler().fit_transform(x)
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, random_state=0)

results = {}
for loss in ("hinge", "logistic"):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    est = OptimizedSVC(loss=loss, cv=5).fit(x_train, y_train)
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0
    f = est.decision_function(x_test)
    p = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-f))  # sigmoid of the decision values (= predict_proba for "logistic")
    results[loss] = p
    print(
        f"{loss:9s} {seconds:5.1f} s  accuracy {est.score(x_test, y_test):.3f}  "
        f"log-loss {log_loss(y_test, p):.3f}  (lam = {est.lam_:.3g})"
    )
Output
hinge       2.5 s  accuracy 0.880  log-loss 0.386  (lam = 0.266)
Output
logistic    4.4 s  accuracy 0.870  log-loss 0.353  (lam = 0.134)

predict_proba returns the probabilities of both classes. A reliability diagram shows how well they are calibrated:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4.5))
for loss, p in results.items():
    frac, mean = calibration_curve(y_test, p, n_bins=8)
    ax.plot(mean, frac, "o-", label=loss)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", label="perfect")
ax.set_xlabel("predicted probability")
ax.set_ylabel("observed frequency")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()

items.title: Low-level API
items.text:
Build a training problem, train it, and evaluate the cross-validation error gradient.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

from optimized_svm import EpsilonInsensitiveLoss, TrainingProblem, cv_error_and_gradient, train
from optimized_svm.validation import SmoothAbsoluteValidation

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(300, 2))
y = np.sin(2 * x[:, 0]) * np.cos(x[:, 1]) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=300)

A smoothed epsilon-SVR with a piecewise cubic smoothing (\(C^2\) loss).

loss = EpsilonInsensitiveLoss(epsilon=0.1, smoothing=0.05, degree="3")
prob = TrainingProblem(x * 0.8, y, loss, lam=1e-3)
sol = train(prob)
print(f"SMO steps {sol.smo_steps}, Newton steps {sol.newton_steps}, residual {sol.residual:.1e}")
Output
SMO steps 3000, Newton steps 13, residual 7.3e-14

The CV error and its exact gradient with respect to \((\log\lambda, \log s)\).

folds = list(KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(x))
theta = np.log([1e-3, 0.8])
res = cv_error_and_gradient(
    theta, x, y, np.ones(len(y)), folds, loss, SmoothAbsoluteValidation(0.1)

print(f"CV error {res.error:.4f}, gradient {res.gradient}")

items.title: Quickstart: gradient-based tuning vs. grid search
items.text:
OptimizedSVC tunes the regularisation lam and the kernel scaling by minimising the cross-validation error with exact gradients. We compare it with GridSearchCV on a noisy classification task.

import time

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC

from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVC

x, y = make_classification(1000, 8, n_informative=4, flip_y=0.05, random_state=0)
x = StandardScaler().fit_transform(x)
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, random_state=0)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
opt = OptimizedSVC(cv=5).fit(x_train, y_train)
t_opt = time.perf_counter() - t0
acc = opt.score(x_test, y_test)
print(
    f"OptimizedSVC: lam = {opt.lam_:.3g}, gamma = {opt.scaling_opt_[0] ** 2:.3g}, "
    f"{len(opt.history_)} CV evaluations, {t_opt:.1f} s, test accuracy {acc:.3f}"
)
Output
OptimizedSVC: lam = 0.205, gamma = 0.153, 16 CV evaluations, 1.8 s, test accuracy 0.844

The grid search needs far more cross-validation evaluations for a comparable result.

grid = {"C": np.logspace(-2, 4, 13), "gamma": np.logspace(-4, 1, 11)}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), grid, cv=5, n_jobs=1).fit(x_train, y_train)
t_grid = time.perf_counter() - t0
best = search.best_params_
print(
    f"GridSearchCV: C = {best['C']:.3g}, gamma = {best['gamma']:.3g}, "
    f"{len(search.cv_results_['params'])} grid points, {t_grid:.1f} s, "
    f"test accuracy {search.score(x_test, y_test):.3f}"
)
Output
GridSearchCV: C = 1, gamma = 0.316, 143 grid points, 10.9 s, test accuracy 0.856

items.title: Bilevel formulation
items.text:
Let \(\theta = (\log\lambda, \log s_1, \dots, \log s_K)\) collect the hyperparameters. For folds \((T_j, V_j)\) the upper level problem is

\[ \min_\theta\; E(\theta) = \frac{1}{|V|}\sum_j \sum_{v \in V_j} L\big(f_j(x_v; \theta), y_v\big), \]

where \(f_j\) is the decision function trained on \(T_j\) (the lower level problem) and \(L\) a smooth validation loss: a smoothed hinge for classification, a Huber-type smoothed absolute error, the squared error or the Poisson loss for regression (Sec. 9.1).

items.title: Implicit function theorem
items.text:
With smoothed losses, the training solution satisfies the (semismooth) optimality system

\[ a_l + \phi_l'(\mathrm{ka}_l + b + s_l c) = 0, \qquad \mathbf 1^\top a = 0, \qquad (s^\top a = A), \]

with \(\mathrm{ka} = K a/\lambda\). Only terms \(P = \{l : \phi_l'' > 0\}\) react to small changes of \(\theta\); all others keep \(a_l\) constant. Differentiating the system on \(P\) gives (Sec. 9.2)

\[ \begin{pmatrix} K_{PP}/\lambda + \operatorname{diag}(1/h_P) & \mathbf 1 & s_P\\ \mathbf 1^\top & 0 & 0\\ s_P^\top & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\partial a_P\\ \partial b\\ \partial c\end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix}\partial_\theta \mathrm{ka}_P\\ 0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad h = \phi''. \]

items.title: Adjoint system
items.text:
Instead of solving this system for every hyperparameter, the chain rule is applied in reverse: one solves the transposed (symmetric) system with right-hand side \((K_{VP}^ op abla L/\lambda,\; \mathbf 1^ op abla L,\; 0)\) for \(u\) and obtains

\[ rac{\partial E}{\partial heta} = -u^ op \partial_ heta \mathrm{ka}_P + abla L^ op \partial_ heta f_V ig|_{a\ ext{fixed}}, \]

with \(\partial_{\log\lambda}\mathrm{ka} = -\mathrm{ka}\) and \(\partial_{\log s_k} K = -2 K \odot D_k\) (\(D_k\): squared distances in block \(k\) of the scaled features). The cost per fold is one factorization of a matrix of size \(|P|\), independent of the number of hyperparameters — this is what makes ARD kernels affordable. For the quadratic smoothing \(h\) is piecewise constant, so the Newton system of the last training step has the same matrix as the adjoint system and its Cholesky factor is reused; for other degrees the matrix is factorized again. Contractions with \(\partial_{\log s_k} K\) do not form the matrices \(D_k\): \(\sum_{ij} W_{ij}\lVert x_{i,B_k} - z_{j,B_k} Vert^2\) is evaluated from row and column sums of \(W\) and one product \(WZ\) for all blocks.

The implementation is tested against central finite differences for all losses, smoothing degrees, ARD blocks and an active \( u\)-constraint (relative error about \(10^{-8}\)).

items.title: Loss parameters (\(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\))
items.text:
The parameters of the loss — the tube width \(\varepsilon\) of the \(\varepsilon\)-insensitive loss and the smoothing width \(\delta\) — enter the optimality condition \(a_l + \phi_l'(t_l; p) = 0\) directly, not through the kernel. The same adjoint vector \(u\) therefore gives their derivatives at no extra cost:

\[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial p} = -\sum_{l \in P} u_l\, \frac{\partial_p \phi_l'(t_l)}{\phi_l''(t_l)} . \]

All smoothings are of the form \(m_\delta(x) = \delta\, m_1(x/\delta)\), hence \(\partial_\delta m_\delta'(x) = -(x/\delta)\, m_\delta''(x)\) for every degree. The ratios are \(s_l\) for \(\varepsilon\) and \(s_l \cdot \mathrm{arg}_l/\delta\) for \(\delta\), where \(\mathrm{arg}_l\) is the argument of the smoothed maximum and \(s_l\) the term sign (for the hinge loss \(y_l\) replaces \(s_l\)). They are implemented as Loss.param_ratio. The function cv_error_and_gradient takes loss_params=("epsilon", "smoothing"); theta is then extended by \(\log\varepsilon\) and \(\log\delta\).

import numpy as np

from optimized_svm import EpsilonInsensitiveLoss, cv_error_and_gradient

theta = np.r_[np.log(lam), np.log(scaling), np.log(0.1), np.log(0.3)]  # lam, s, eps, delta
res = cv_error_and_gradient(
    theta, x, y, w, folds, EpsilonInsensitiveLoss(0.1, 0.3), validation,
    loss_params=("epsilon", "smoothing"),
)

The gradients are exact (checked against finite differences, also for \(\delta\) down to 0.003), but the estimators do not tune these parameters, because it rarely pays off:

  • \(\varepsilon\) is not identifiable for \(\varepsilon < \delta\) (quadratic smoothing): the two smoothed sides overlap and \(\varepsilon\) only shifts the loss by a constant, so the solution, the CV error and the gradient do not depend on it.
  • The CV error is multimodal in \(\delta\) (variations of about 1 %) and rough for very small \(\delta\); starting with a large \(\varepsilon\) (everything inside the tube, zero solution) can end in a poor basin.
  • On data without outliers the tuned parameters do not improve the CV error. With 8 % gross outliers a smaller \(\delta\) helps (test MSE 0.226 → 0.216), but a fixed small \(\delta\) does as well, at a fraction of the cost (tuning needs two to four times as many CV evaluations).

The study is benchmarks/hpo_loss_params.py.

items.title: Optimization
items.text: L-BFGS-B runs on \(\theta\) within box constraints. Each evaluation warm-starts SMO with the fold solutions of the previous evaluation (about ten times fewer SMO steps for regression). With time_limit, the best parameters found so far are used.

items.title: Subspace SVM
items.text:
The model is restricted to the span of \(m\) basis points \(z_1,\dots,z_m\) (thesis, Sec. 5.3):

\[ w = \sum_j \beta_j \phi(z_j), \qquad f(x) = \sum_j \beta_j\, k(x, z_j) + b . \]

items.title: Training
items.text:
By Corollary 5.9 the dual is the standard dual with the projected kernel \(K_s = K_{XZ} K_{ZZ}^{-1} K_{ZX}\) (a Nyström approximation). Equivalently the SVM has the explicit feature map \(\psi(x) = L^{-1} k_Z(x)\) with \(K_{ZZ} = L L^\top\), and the primal problem has only \(m+1\) unknowns:

\[ \min_{u,b}\ \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|u\|^2 + \sum_l \varphi_l(\psi_{k(l)}^\top u + b), \qquad \beta = L^{-\top} u . \]

It is solved by a damped Newton method with systems of size \(m+1\); one step costs \(O(nm^2 + m^3)\) instead of a factorization of size \(n\). SMO is not used, so the loss must have positive curvature somewhere (smoothing > 0, squared, logistic, Poisson); smoothing = 0 is rejected.

items.title: Hypergradient
items.text: The stationarity conditions in \((\beta, b)\) define the solution implicitly. One adjoint system of size \(m+1\) per fold gives the gradient of the cross-validation error with respect to \(\log\lambda\) and the log kernel scalings (including ARD blocks). It is checked against central differences for the smoothed hinge, ε-insensitive (degrees 2/3/6), logistic and squared loss.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
All four estimators take n_basis and basis_tol:

from optimized_svm import OptimizedSVR

est = OptimizedSVR(n_basis="auto", basis_tol=1.0).fit(X, y)   # basis size from the residual rule
est = OptimizedSVR(n_basis=200).fit(X, y)                      # fixed size
  • n_basis=None (default): full model. An integer: that many basis points. "auto": select_basis with tolerance basis_tol (see below); if the limit \(n/10\) is hit, a warning is issued and the full model is used.
  • Needs a smooth loss (smoothing > 0, or squared/logistic/Poisson) and no max_asum. Models are trained by Newton's method only (newton_options; smo_options is ignored).
  • The optimizers (OptimizedSVC/SVR) choose the basis of every fold at the starting values of each stage (global scaling, then ARD scalings) and keep it fixed during L-BFGS-B, so the objective stays smooth. With n_basis="auto" the rule is then checked at the result (nystroem_residual(x_scaled, idx) / lam <= basis_tol in every fold); if it fails, e.g. because the optimizer lowered \(\lambda\) by orders of magnitude, a new basis is chosen there and L-BFGS-B restarts (at most 5 rounds per stage). The stage keeps the best evaluation of its last round (earlier rounds used smaller subspaces and are not comparable); history_ entries carry basis_round. An integer n_basis is never re-selected. The final model is trained on all data with a basis chosen at the optimized hyperparameters. After fitting, basis_ holds its indices, support_/dual_coef_ the basis points and expansion coefficients, and history_ records n_basis per evaluation.
  • Low-level: pass basis (one index array per fold, indices into x) to cv_error_and_gradient; warm_start then holds expansion coefficients. loss_params and max_asum are not supported with a basis.

n_basis=\"auto\" often falls back to the full model with the default starting values

The basis is chosen at the starting values of each stage. With the defaults (lam_init=1e-2, scaling_init="auto") the residual rule did not hold within \(n/10\) points for ε-SVR on Friedman #1 with \(n = 5000\), so all three variants (tol 1, tol 10, full) ran the full model and gave identical results (17 evaluations, about 520 s each; benchmarks/results/subspace_hpo_n5000_fallback.json). A warning is issued, but no speed-up results. The gain shown below was measured at wide kernels (scale 0.05–0.1) and \(\lambda \ge 10^{-2}\); start the optimization there (scaling_init, lam_init) if you want the subspace model to be used. An end-to-end comparison of the optimization with such starting values is still open.

items.title: Choosing the basis
items.text:
Study benchmarks/subspace_params.py (raw data benchmarks/results/subspace_params.json): ε-SVR and classification on Friedman-type data, \(n = 1000\) and \(2500\), three kernel scales, \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-1}\), 5 folds, basis sizes 25–800; the cross-validation error of one evaluation is compared with the full model.

  • Selection rule: greedy pivoted Cholesky, not random. At equal \(m\) the two rules give about the same error (median excess over the full model at \(m = 400\): +0.4 % pivoted, +0.7 % random on regression), so the choice does not matter for quality; pivoted Cholesky is used because it yields the residual trace needed for the size rule.
  • Size rule: stop when \(\operatorname{tr}(K - K_s) \le au\lambda\). The trace of the Nyström residual relative to \(\lambda\) predicts the loss of accuracy, the trace alone does not (with small \(\lambda\) a residual of \(10^{-3}\,n\) already costs +55 % error). Excess CV error over the full model, all 24 settings × 6 sizes:
\(\operatorname{tr}(K-K_s)/\lambda\) runs median maximum < 1 24 +0.01 % +0.9 % 1–10 10 +0.6 % +11 % 10–100 15 +2 % +14 % 100–1000 18 +15 % +82 % > 1000 65 +17 % to +28 % +135 %

select_basis(x_scaled, lam, tol=1.0, max_size=None) implements this with \(\tau = 1\) (use tol=10 to accept up to ~14 %). The default size limit is \(\max(10, n/10)\); if it is hit, the returned ratio is above tol and the model is not a close approximation. - Check of the rule (select_basis with the size limit \(n/4\), \(n = 2500\), one evaluation incl. 5 folds; excess = CV error over the full model):

items.title: Switching from SMO to Newton
items.text: Training first runs SMO on the dual up to a rough tolerance and then refines the result with Newton's method (see Training problem). The thesis leaves open when to switch (Ch. 11). A late switch wastes SMO steps that Newton would do better; an early switch hands Newton a poor starting point, so it needs more steps, each of which factorizes the matrix of the terms with positive curvature. This page summarizes a measurement study; the script is benchmarks/smo_newton_switch.py.

items.title: Rule
items.text: By default SMO stops when the violation measure is at most ROUGH_SMO_TOL = 0.3 or after ROUGH_SMO_STEPS = 5 steps per loss term, whichever comes first. If Newton's method fails, an accurate SMO solution (tolerance \(10^{-6}\), no budget) is computed instead. Passing tol or max_steps in smo_options replaces these defaults.

items.title: Findings
items.text:
Total time of one training (SMO plus Newton) for tolerances from \(10^{-3}\) to "no SMO", on 40 problems (ε-SVR and classification; \(n\) from 300 to 3000; \(\lambda\) from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-1}\); kernel width, smoothing \(\delta\) and degree varied; with and without an active 1-norm bound), cold start and as a warm-started step of a hyperparameter optimization. Newton's method never failed.

  • A tolerance of about 0.3 is best on average. Relative to the best tolerance of each problem (geometric mean), 0.3 costs 1.12 (classification) and 1.20 (regression) in cold starts, 0.1 costs 1.16 and 1.35, and \(10^{-3}\) costs 1.3 and 2.2. Tolerances of 3 or more are 2.2 to 5.8 times slower: Newton then starts almost from zero and needs 8 to 35 steps.
  • Small \(\lambda\) prefers an earlier hand-over. SMO needs many steps when \(\lambda\) is small (for classification with \(n = 1000\) about 80 000 steps at tolerance 0.1 for \(\lambda = 10^{-4}\)), while Newton's cost hardly depends on \(\lambda\). For classification the best tolerance rises from about 0.01 (\(\lambda = 10^{-1}\)) to 1 (\(\lambda \le 10^{-3}\)); for regression it is about 0.03 for \(\lambda = 10^{-1}\) and between 0.1 and 1 for smaller \(\lambda\).
  • A narrow kernel prefers a later hand-over (classification). For large scalings the kernel matrix is close to the identity, SMO is cheap and Newton's method needs more steps from a rough start (best tolerance \(10^{-3}\) for four times the default scaling).
  • Little influence: \(n\) (300 to 3000), the smoothing parameter \(\delta\), the degree (2, 3, 6), the working set rule, shrinking, one- or two-sided search and the stopping criterion. The bound-aware criterion with \(\rho = 1\) saves 10–25 % of the SMO steps at a tolerance of 0.3. The number of BLAS threads changes the absolute times but not the optimum (0.3 for ε-SVR with \(n = 3000\) with one and with twelve threads).
  • A step budget removes the worst cases. SMO can converge extremely slowly, in particular when the 1-norm bound (ν-type constraint) is active (zig-zagging between the two sign groups) and for very small \(\lambda\). Newton's method solves these problems in one or two steps. With the budget the worst case relative to the best rule drops from 2.1 to 1.3 (classification, cold) and from 12 to 3.3 (regression, warm-started step).

items.title: Standard training problem
items.text:
For samples \((x_i, y_i)\), a feature map \(\varphi\) with kernel \(k(x, z) = \langle\varphi(x),\varphi(z)\rangle\) and convex losses \(\ell_i\), the standard training problem (Strasdat, Def. 2.5) reads

\[ \min_{w, b}\; \frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\langle w, \varphi(x_i)\rangle + b). \]

Its Fenchel dual is (Cor. 3.11)

\[ \min_{\alpha}\; \frac{1}{2\lambda}\alpha^\top K \alpha + \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i^\star(-\alpha_i) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf 1^\top\alpha = 0, \]

and \(w = \frac1\lambda \sum_i \alpha_i \varphi(x_i)\) (representer theorem). The decision function is \(f(x) = \frac1\lambda\sum_i \alpha_i k(x, x_i) + b\).

items.title: Smoothed losses
items.text:
Hinge and \(\varepsilon\)-insensitive losses are built from \(\max(0, t)\). Replacing it by a smooth approximation \(m_\delta\) that agrees with \(\max(0, t)\) for \(|t| \ge \delta\) (Sec. 4.4) yields differentiable losses. For the quadratic smoothing

\[ m_\delta(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & t \le -\delta\\ \frac{(t+\delta)^2}{4\delta} & |t| < \delta \\ t & t \ge \delta\end{cases} \]

the conjugate is quadratic on an interval, so the dual is still a box-constrained QP that SMO solves exactly. The higher degree variants ("3", "6") are \(C^2\).

items.title: Two-step training
items.text:
1. SMO (smo-solver) solves the dual with quadratic smoothing to a rough tolerance (Ch. 7). Working set selection uses second-order information and shrinking removes variables fixed at their bounds.
  2. Semismooth Newton (Ch. 8.4) solves the optimality system of the actual (possibly higher-degree) smoothed problem

$$ a + \ell'(\tfrac1\lambda K a + b\mathbf 1 + s c) = 0, \qquad \mathbf 1^\top a = 0 $$

Terms with vanishing curvature (\(\ell'' = 0\)) are fixed explicitly, so only a linear system on the terms with \(\ell'' > 0\) has to be solved. Usually one to a few steps suffice.

The SMO stage can be tuned with smo_options (all options of smo-solver), for instance the bound-aware stopping criterion of Sec. 7.6, smo_options={"stopping": "bound_aware"}. By default SMO runs to the rough tolerance tol = 0.3 or for at most five steps per loss term; see Switching from SMO to Newton for the reasons.

For non-smooth losses (\(\delta = 0\)) only SMO is used; for losses without an SMO formulation (squared, logistic, Poisson) Newton starts at zero.

items.title: Logistic loss
items.text: The logistic loss \(\ell(t) = \log(1 + e^{-yt})\) (Sec. 4.1.3) is smooth without any smoothing and its curvature \(\ell''(t) = \sigma(-yt)\,\sigma(yt)\) is positive everywhere. Its conjugate involves \(x \log x\) (an entropy), so the dual is not a separable quadratic and SMO cannot be used. Newton's method works as usual (about 5–9 steps from zero), but because no term has vanishing curvature the solution is dense and every Newton system has the full size \(n\) (cost \(\mathcal O(n^3)\) per step). In exchange the decision values have a probabilistic reading, \(P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(f(x))\), used by predict_proba. On the checkerboard-like test sets of the benchmarks its accuracy matches the smoothed hinge loss, the test log-loss is slightly better, and training is 3–6 times slower at \(n = 2000\). Starting Newton at the solution of neighbouring hyperparameters does not help: the dual coefficients \(a = -\ell'(f)\) change with the kernel, so the previous \(a\) is no better than zero.

items.title: Optional 1-norm constraint
items.text: max_asum=A adds \(\sum_i |\alpha_i| \le A\) (a generalized \(\nu\)-SVM, Sec. 5.2). Its multiplier \(c \ge 0\) shifts the decision values of the training terms by \(s_i c\).
